naslov: The group chat that bonds Black NBA coaches off the court
tekst:
DETROIT PISTONS COACH J.B. Bickerstaff and then-Orlando Magic coach Jamahl Mosley broke the ice after nearly two weeks of silence: a simple bro hug at midcourt before their teams played Game 7 of last season first-round series.
More than a series was on the line -- jobs have been decided in these situations, and that series was no different. Regardless, the two consider themselves brothers.
"We didn't make eye contact during the series," Bickerstaff said. "I knew the outcome of that series -- we played two years before when I was in Cleveland -- if I would've lost to Jamahl, I would've been fired. I knew if Jamahl didn't beat us [last season], he was going to be fired.
"Coaching those games was extremely emotional, and them both coming down to Game 7s adds more weight to those moments. I know the impact that it has on you, your wife in that moment. His kids call me Uncle."
Several coaches closely watched the matchup. They are part of an 11-member group chat featuring Black NBA head coaches and assistants who have been friends for years.
"For us, it was fun," Indiana Pacers associate head coach Lloyd Pierce said. "It was Game 7. You don't have to put that face on anymore for your players. They knew. This is results oriented. Someone's going home, someone ain't. But it's all love. They had to be professionals, but it was a beautiful moment for our group."
Pierce and Washington Wizards assistant David Vanterpool couldn't wait to show the video of the two close friends' hug before the game at their annual "wine and conversation" event that takes place during summer league. It exemplified the community they have striven to create: two fierce competitors in their natural element who, behind the scenes, are friends in any other group chat, commiserating over shared experiences and struggles, talking about issues of the world in a space where they knew it would stay without judgment.
And doing so with the only men who can identify with what they are going through: each other.
There are nine Black head coaches in the NBA -- three fewer than last season with Jason Kidd, Chauncey Billups and Doc Rivers no longer with their franchises. When Kidd and Boston's Joe Mazzulla met in the 2024 NBA Finals, it was the first time two Black coaches faced each other in the Finals since 1975, when Al Attles' Golden State Warriors swept K.C. Jones' Washington Bullets. It's been cyclical, but the NBA had recently reached a high mark for Black coaches. There were 15 in 2022-23 and 14 the following season. In the 2019-20 season, that number was just seven.
This collective, which as a group chat has expanded into other events, has become an outlet to discuss opportunities that have come and ones that haven't. But it has also expanded into a network of support and connections that extends far beyond the court. The connections are so intertwined -- coaches who have served under one another and been introduced through members of the group chat -- it's almost too many to name.
"It's the most important thing we have in this business," Bickerstaff said. "Like nothing gets done in the NBA without connections and community. So like us being able to build a community has changed the outlook and the window of opportunity for people."
Hours after Bickerstaff and Mosley embraced ahead of their Game 7 meeting, the top-seeded Pistons beat the eighth-seeded Magic, completing a comeback from being down 3-1 in the series. Shortly after, Bickerstaff's thoughts drifted to Mosley and his future.
"You're extremely excited about what's next for you, and you have to prepare for that," Bickerstaff said. "But you're also walking around with the weight of what happens to someone you care about."
Mosley was fired 24 hours later. Two weeks later, the New Orleans Pelicans hired him.
NO ONE CAN REMEMBER  when the group chat started, who started it or even the original coaches who were in it -- some were added after the initial iteration.
What they all agreed on was how quickly it became a place for coaches at different stages of their lives and careers to vent, seek advice, talk about the world and do so freely.
New York Knicks coach Mike Brown is the oldest at 56. Charlotte Hornets assistant coach John Bryant (not to be confused with Cleveland Cavaliers assistant coach Johnnie Bryant, who's also part of the group chat) is the youngest, not yet 40. It also includes Bickerstaff, Mosley, Pierce, Vanterpool, former Memphis Grizzlies and Knicks coach David Fizdale, Philadelphia 76ers assistant Phil Handy, former Los Angeles Lakers coach and current Milwaukee Bucks assistant Darvin Ham and Wizards assistant J.J. Outlaw.
Like any group chat, there are jokes -- and nobody is off-limits.
Brown's viral demand and demonstration, showing Sacramento Kings players what it's like to sprint back on defense ("turn the f---ing jets on!") made the rounds.
"We gave Mike s--- about that for two hours," Pierce said of Brown's moment in Sacramento.
Fizdale's "take that for data" slam during the 2017 NBA playoffs when he was coaching the Grizzlies against the San Antonio Spurs was another moment, both for its seriousness and its virality.
"If you do something and somebody finds a clip and puts it out there, make no mistake," Pierce said. "Fiz went viral and next thing you know someone makes a light skin joke and it's not about the clip anymore. It's about the jokes now. Classic group chat stuff."
The friendships started with hoops and Hall of Famer Tim Grgurich's annual basketball camp in Las Vegas. Those four-day summer sessions were a place for the league to convene and for upward of 50 young players and 30 coaches to sharpen their tools. Younger coaches worked one-on-one with current players and also met with older coaches to network. After a long day of work, the coaches would hang out late into the night.
